title: SSH Config
summary: Give servers short nicknames in ~/.ssh/config and test it without connecting.
intro:
Typing ssh -p 2222 -i ~/.ssh/id_academy student@192.168.1.50 every time is no fun.
The file ~/.ssh/config lets you give a server a nickname, so later you just type: ssh myserver
In this lesson you write that file line by line. Nothing connects anywhere, it's only a text file.
The .ssh folder is already there for you.
outro: Your SSH config is ready! With a real server, ssh myserver would now use the right address, user, port and key all by itself. Pro tip: you can have many Host blocks in one config file, one for each computer.

steps.instruction: Create the file .ssh/config with the line: Host myserver
hints: echo prints text, and > writes it into a file (a new file, or it replaces the old content).
steps.explain: Host starts a block for one server, and myserver is the nickname. All the lines after it (until the next Host line) are settings for this nickname.

steps.instruction: Add the real address of the server: the line   HostName 192.168.1.50   (two spaces at the start).
hints: Careful: > would replace the file. Use >> to add a line at the end. The spaces at the start are only there to make it easy to read.
steps.explain: HostName is the real address: an IP address like 192.168.1.50, or a name like pi.local or example.com. The nickname is only for you.

steps.instruction: Add two more lines: the user name   User student   and the port   Port 2222
hints: Two echo commands, both with >>. Check your work with: cat .ssh/config
Type: echo '  User student' >> .ssh/config   and then:   echo '  Port 2222' >> .ssh/config
steps.explain: User is the account name on the server. Port is the 'door number': the normal SSH port is 22, but some servers use another one.

steps.instruction: Tell SSH which key to use for this server. Add the line   IdentityFile ~/.ssh/id_academy
hints: Same as before: echo with >>. Use single quotes, so the ~ stays a ~ in the file.
steps.explain: IdentityFile points to your PRIVATE key (the file without .pub), like the one you made in the last lesson. Now SSH knows which key belongs to which server.

steps.instruction: Protect your config: make it readable and writable only by you (mode 600).
hints: 6 = read + write for you, 0 for the group, 0 for everyone else.
steps.explain: If other people could change your config, they could send you to a fake server. That's why SSH may refuse a config file that others can write. Look at it with ls -l .ssh: you should see -rw-------.

steps.instruction: Bonus: ask SSH what it WOULD do for myserver, without connecting. Show only the lines for hostname, user and port.
hints: ssh -F picks the config file, and -G means 'only print the settings, don't connect'. A pipe into grep filters the long list.
steps.explain: SSH read your nickname and found the real address, user and port. (A note about 'Pseudo-terminal' is normal here, you can ignore it.) The first time you really connect to a server, SSH asks 'Are you sure you want to continue connecting?' and saves the server's key in ~/.ssh/known_hosts. Next time it checks that key, which protects you from fake servers.
